title: Tdhtdhtdhtdhtdh: Sound Effects!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) explore sound effects for film and TV: the difference between diegetic and non-diegetic sound, why most on-screen non-dialogue sound is added in post-production, and the craft of Foley artistry named after Jack Foley. They cover early vaudeville and silent-film traps, Jack Foley's career at Universal (Showboat, Spartacus), the Foley studio setup, and the roughly hundred Foley artists working in the US today. They then discuss famous sound tricks: the Wilhelm Scream and Ben Burtt's Star Wars work, ET's walking sounds, Titanic's floating-door/hair sound, Fight Club punches, the melon stabbing in Berberian Sound Studio, Jurassic Park's egg hatch, Raiders boulder, Star Wars blaster and tie fighter sounds, Chewbacca and R2-D2, and sound in nature documentaries. The episode closes with budget context, merch news, and a listener correction email about Teen Vogue. Includes personal banter and laser tag anecdotes.

segments.title: Opening banter and sound effects overview
segments.summary: Josh and the iHeart Intro voice banter about the episode, then introduce sound effects and explain that most non-dialogue sound in live-action film is added in post-production by Foley artists or from sound libraries.

segments.title: Why Foley artists matter and on-set sound
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Foley artists act along with actors to create sounds, how sound departments are often sidelined on set, and why location sets are shot silently with sounds added later.

segments.title: Diegetic sound and sound recording
segments.summary: Josh defines diegetic sound as sound inside the movie's world, contrasted with non-diegetic score and narration. The hosts discuss sound designers recording their own sounds in the field and sweetening library sounds with layers.

segments.title: Creating unusual sounds and footsteps
segments.summary: The hosts note sound designers create invented sounds for sci-fi, and that footsteps must be performed to match each actor's weight and gait rather than taken from libraries. Budget often determines whether Foley is used.

segments.title: Vaudeville and early traps
segments.summary: The hosts trace live sound effects back to vaudeville and silent-film accompaniment, describing traps (sound-effect contraptions) made by companies such as Ludwig for percussionists to imitate sounds.

segments.title: Live silent-film sound performers and slapstick origin
segments.summary: Josh describes Nick White's live sound effects for vintage films and the hosts mention Josh Harmon's cartoon sound videos on Instagram. Josh explains the slapstick trap is the origin of the term slapstick.

segments.title: Transition to talkies and The Jazz Singer
segments.summary: The hosts describe The Jazz Singer as the first widely successful talkie and explain Warner Brothers' Vitaphone, which synced audio to the projector using discs.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to the episode.

segments.title: Laser tag and machine gun mouth sounds banter
segments.summary: Personal banter about making machine gun sounds with the mouth and anecdotes about playing laser tag.

segments.title: Jack Foley's career and the Showboat talkie conversion
segments.summary: Jack Foley's career is profiled: he wrote a monthly column for Universal, worked as an insert director, and became a sound effects artist whose name became the term Foley. The hosts describe him adding sound to Showboat at Universal's Stage ten, recorded live in one take to the Vitaphone disc.

segments.title: Foley room history and uncredited work
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Foley's room becoming the standard Foley room, Foley never receiving on-screen credit, and Desilu reportedly being the first studio outside Universal to name its room a Foley room in the early sixties.

segments.title: Spartacus armor sound story
segments.summary: Stanley Kubrick reportedly disliked the Roman army marching audio for Spartacus. Jack Foley recreated the armor clanking with car keys, saving a costly reshoot.

segments.title: Foley artists today and their specialized language
segments.summary: The hosts estimate about one hundred Foley artists work in the US today, describe their keen hearing, invented vocabulary, and a New Yorker profile of their work.

segments.title: Foley teams, mixers and process
segments.summary: Foley is usually done in pairs with a Foley mixer making final decisions. Jack Foley pioneered using canes with shoes to simulate multiple walkers.

segments.title: Foley studio floors, props and detail
segments.summary: The hosts describe Foley studio floors with different surfaces, substitutes like reel-to-reel tape for leaves, a tin man mask anecdote, and David Fincher's attention to sound detail such as leather couches.

segments.title: Foley room props and sound-first naming
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Foley stage as a room full of props named for the sound they make, and encourage viewers to watch Foley artist videos.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to the episode.

segments.title: Famous movie sound tricks: Wilhelm Scream, ET, Titanic, Fight Club
segments.summary: The Wilhelm Scream is traced from Distant Drums through The Charge at Feather River to Star Wars, where Ben Burtt adopted it and it appeared in over four hundred films. Other tricks include ET's squishy walk made from Jell-O, wet T-shirt and raw liver, frozen lettuce for Kate Winslet's hair in Titanic, and chicken carcasses and walnuts for punches in Fight Club.

segments.title: Berberian Sound Studio melon stabbing and Jurassic Park egg
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the film Berberian Sound Studio, with Toby Jones as a Foley artist, where a melon stabbing was used for sound. They also mention the Jurassic Park dinosaur egg hatching made from a hand in melon and cracking ice cream cone.

segments.title: Raiders boulder and Star Wars blaster sound origin
segments.summary: The Raiders of the Lost Ark boulder was a car with no motor rolled down a hill. Ben Burtt's blaster sound came from hitting radio tower guy-wire cables with a rock and a metal object, combining recordings from Pocono and Mojave towers.
topics: Raiders of the Lost Ark boulder

segments.title: Tie fighter, Chewbacca and R2-D2 sounds
segments.summary: Tie fighter sounds came from layered and distorted African elephant roars. Chewbacca combined walrus, badger, and bear sounds. R2-D2's beeps and boops were made on an early Moog synthesizer, conveying emotion.

segments.title: Nature documentary sound
segments.summary: The hosts discuss nature documentaries adding sound effects because long-lens filming captures no usable audio, and note that mushrooms, northern lights and spiders make no sound.

segments.title: Sound budgets and the Academy Awards
segments.summary: The hosts explain that sound is often around ten percent of a film budget, music rights can consume budget, and large films can afford full Foley teams, which is why sound gets highlighted at the Academy Awards.

segments.title: Closing banter on enjoying movies
segments.summary: Brief banter about whether Foley artists can enjoy movies, compared to chefs enjoying food.

segments.title: Merch announcement
segments.summary: The hosts announce a new Stuff You Should Know T-shirt store on Cotton Bureau and a shirt slogan idea.

segments.title: Listener correction about Teen Vogue
segments.summary: Stephanie writes to correct the hosts' surprise that Teen Vogue covered the police, noting Teen Vogue is known for serious journalism, and links a Jezebel article.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and information on how to contact the show and find more iHeartRadio podcasts.
